newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African exports seen strong despite rand rally.
newsitem.headline: S.African exports seen strong despite rand rally.

text.p: South African exports are expected to remain strong in 1997 despite the rand's rally against the dollar and other major currencies since the beginning of the year, economists said on Tuesday.
South African exporters still had an advantage in the country's major markets in Europe and the United States because the rand has not regained even half the value it lost last year, they said.

"The rand depreciated 28 to 30 percent last year. We have in no way recouped that loss, so it's still a relatively cheap currency which means we still retain some of our advantage in overseas markets," said Penny Hawkins, an economist with the South African Chamber of Business.

"The rand has gone up about eight percent (against the dollar) since last November, effectively one can still say that compared to last year it's still devalued 20 percent which is still more than inflation parity. That's an indicator that exports should be stronger," she told Reuters.

The local currency has been on an upward march since the beginning of the year on the back of strong foreign demand for South African bonds, bolstering hopes that rand's fortunes have finally turned after a dismal performance in 1996.
On Tuesday, it firmed to below 4.39 against the dollar for the first time since July 1996.
One treasury economist at a leading bank who asked not to be identified said the rand's revival might put a cap on the most optimistic export forecasts anticipated at the end of last year.

However, most of the analysts said although the rand was showing a surprisingly strong rally, they still forecast it to depreciate slowly over the year and said this augured well for exports and the trade balance.

"For the country to achieve stable growth rates of five to six percent that the government is aiming for, we need export-led growth and we won't get that with a strong currency," said ING Barings economist Hania Farhan.
"My forecasts are assuming an eight to 10 percent depreciation over the year. We are likely to see a surplus of $3 billion on the trade account," she said.

Farhan and the other analysts said forecasts of a strong global economy this year should also keep the trade balance healthy. Import demand would be checked as consumers felt the pinch of high domestic interest rates and slowing economy in 1997.

In 1996, the 23 percent depreciation of the trade-weighted rand helped South Africa post a 10.577 billion rand ($2.4 billion) trade surplus for the year -- more than double the 1995 total of 4.884 billion rand.
One sector which will suffer from the strong rand is the gold mining industry, already labouring with a dollar bullion price which is the lowest in more than three years.
With the South African currency powering ahead, rand gold prices have fallen the their lowest levels in 11 months, crimping mines' profits and export earnings.
"If the gold price doesn't go up this year the country may lose $300 to $500 million in revenue," said Farhan.

But gold -- while still important -- no longer plays such a central role in the South African economy. Its contribution to total export earnings fell to 23.1 percent in 1995 from 42.5 percent in 1986, according to the government's Minerals Bureau.
